questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A stack of exactly 100 identical sheets of paper is measured to be 2.25 cm thick. The thickness of one sheet, written with the correct number of significant figures, is:

solution.concept: Significant figures when a measured value is divided by an exact number
solution.explanation: The number of sheets, 100, is a count and so an exact number with unlimited significant figures. The result therefore keeps the three significant figures of the measured thickness 2.25 cm.
steps: Thickness of one sheet = 2.25 cm / 100 = 0.0225 cm
100 is exact, so the result has as many significant figures as 2.25, i.e. three: 0.0225 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.02 cm treats 100 as having only one significant figure; 0.023 cm wrongly rounds to two significant figures; 0.02250 cm adds a fourth significant figure that the measurement does not have.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', significant figures (exact numbers in a calculation)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (its dimensional formula). A stands for the dimension of electric current.

List-I:
A. Electrical resistance
B. Magnetic field (magnetic induction) B
C. Magnetic flux
D. Self-inductance

List-II:
I. [M L² T⁻² A⁻¹]
II. [M L² T⁻³ A⁻²]
III. [M L² T⁻² A⁻²]
IV. [M T⁻² A⁻¹]

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dimensional formulae built step by step from defining relations
solution.explanation: Start from relations whose dimensions are known. Potential difference is work per unit charge, [M L² T⁻²]/[A T] = [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]; resistance is V/I. The magnetic force on a moving charge is F = qvB, so B = F/(qv). Flux is B × area, and self-inductance is flux per unit current (Φ = LI).
steps: V = W/q → [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]; R = V/I → [M L² T⁻³ A⁻²] (II)
B = F/(qv) = [M L T⁻²]/([A T][L T⁻¹]) = [M T⁻² A⁻¹] (IV)
Φ = B × area → [M L² T⁻² A⁻¹] (I)
solution.shortcut: Flux and inductance differ only by one power of A; resistance is the only one with T⁻³.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap flux with inductance (they differ by A⁻¹), or swap resistance with inductance, which share M L² A⁻² but differ in the power of T.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensional formulae and dimensional equations
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The positions of the two ends of a rod on a metre scale are read as (20.0 ± 0.1) cm and (45.0 ± 0.1) cm. The length x of the rod is the difference of the two readings. The maximum percentage error in the quantity x² is:

solution.concept: Error in a difference, then error in a power
solution.explanation: When two quantities are subtracted, their absolute errors add: x = (25.0 ± 0.2) cm. When a quantity is raised to a power n, its relative error is multiplied by n.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.8% is the error in x itself (the square is forgotten); 1.4% adds the percentage errors of the two readings (0.5% + 0.22%) and doubles them, but errors of a difference must be added as absolute errors; 0.4% takes Δx as 0.1 cm and forgets to double for the square.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The diameter of a wire is measured five times with a screw gauge, giving 2.02 mm, 1.98 mm, 2.03 mm, 1.97 mm and 2.00 mm. Taking the mean absolute error as the error in the diameter, the percentage error in the area of cross-section of the wire, calculated as πd²/4, is:

solution.concept: Mean value, mean absolute error and the error in a squared quantity
solution.explanation: The best estimate is the arithmetic mean; the mean absolute error is the mean of the magnitudes of the deviations. The area depends on d², so its relative error is twice that of d (π/4 is exact).
solution.why_others_wrong: 1% is the error in the diameter, not the area; 4% multiplies the relative error by 4 (the 4 in πd²/4 is exact and adds no error); 0.5% halves the relative error instead of doubling it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', absolute error, relative error and percentage error

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A stone is dropped from rest from the top of a building 45 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the speed with which it hits the ground is:

solution.concept: Uniformly accelerated motion: v² = u² + 2as
solution.explanation: For free fall from rest, u = 0 and a = g, so v² = 2gh.
solution.shortcut: Time of fall √(2h/g) = 3 s, and v = gt = 30 m/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 m/s is half the speed (v = gt/2 confuses average and final speed); 45 m/s takes v numerically equal to h; 30√2 m/s uses v² = 4gh.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For the vectors A = 3î + 4ĵ and B = 4î − 3ĵ, match List-I (quantity) with List-II (its value).

List-I:
A. A · B
B. |A × B|
C. |A + B|
D. |A|

List-II:
I. 5
II. 0
III. 5√2
IV. 25

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Scalar product, vector product and magnitude of vectors in component form
solution.explanation: A · B = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y. For vectors in the x–y plane, A × B = (AₓB_y − A_yBₓ) k̂. The magnitude of a vector is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components.
steps: A · B = 3 × 4 + 4 × (−3) = 0 (II): the vectors are perpendicular
solution.shortcut: Since A ⊥ B and |A| = |B| = 5, |A × B| = 5 × 5 = 25 and |A + B| = 5√2 at once.
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping the dot and cross products is the usual slip; the other codes put |A + B| = 5 (adding magnitudes wrongly) or interchange 5√2 and 25.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', addition of vectors and resolution; scalar and vector products
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle moves with constant speed around a circle. Over the time it takes to go round the circle exactly once, its average velocity and its average acceleration are:

solution.concept: Average velocity and average acceleration over a closed path
solution.explanation: Average velocity is (net displacement)/(time) and average acceleration is (change in velocity)/(time). After one full revolution the particle is back at its starting point (zero displacement) and has the same velocity, in magnitude and direction, as at the start (zero change in velocity). Both averages are therefore zero, even though the instantaneous acceleration v²/r is never zero.
steps: Net displacement in one revolution = 0 → average velocity = 0
Final velocity = initial velocity → Δv = 0 → average acceleration = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: v²/r is the magnitude of the instantaneous (centripetal) acceleration, not its average over a revolution; 2πr/T is the average speed, not the average velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', uniform circular motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle moves along the x-axis so that its velocity at position x is v = 3x, where v is in m/s and x in metres. Its acceleration when it is at x = 2 m is:

solution.concept: Acceleration from velocity given as a function of position: a = v (dv/dx)
solution.explanation: By the chain rule, a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v (dv/dx). Here dv/dx = 3, so a = 3v = 9x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 m/s² takes dv/dx alone as the acceleration; 6 m/s² is the velocity at x = 2 m; 9 m/s² is the value of 9x at x = 1 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Rain is falling with a speed of 20 m/s at an angle of 30° with the vertical, its horizontal component of velocity being towards the east. A man walks on a level road. The velocity with which he must walk so that the rain appears to him to fall vertically, and the speed of the rain relative to him, are respectively:

solution.concept: Relative velocity in two dimensions
solution.explanation: The velocity of the rain relative to the man is v_rain − v_man. For it to be vertical, the man's velocity must cancel the horizontal component of the rain's velocity, so he must walk east at that component. What is left is the vertical component of the rain's velocity.
steps: Horizontal component of rain = 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s (east)
Man walks east at 10 m/s → relative velocity = 10√3 m/s vertically downward
solution.why_others_wrong: Walking west would double the horizontal relative component; 10√3 m/s east uses cos 30° for the horizontal component; 20 m/s is the speed relative to the ground, not relative to the man.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 10 m/s towards the east, 10√3 m/s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The position vector of a particle moving in the x–y plane is r = (4t) î + (t²) ĵ, where r is in metres and t in seconds. At t = 2 s, the angle between its velocity and its acceleration is:

solution.concept: Velocity and acceleration as derivatives of the position vector
solution.explanation: v = dr/dt and a = dv/dt; the angle between them follows from cos θ = (v · a)/(|v||a|).
steps: v = 4 î + 2t ĵ → at t = 2 s, v = 4î + 4ĵ m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 90° would hold only at t = 0, when v = 4î; 0° would need v along ĵ; 60° comes from a wrong magnitude of v.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A projectile launched from level ground moves along the path y = x − 0.05x², where x (horizontal) and y (vertical) are in metres, measured from the point of projection. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The angle of projection is 45° above the horizontal.
(b) The speed of projection is 10√2 m/s.
(c) The horizontal range is 20 m.
(d) The maximum height reached is 10 m.
(e) The time of flight is 2√2 s.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Reading a projectile's speed and angle from its trajectory equation
solution.explanation: The trajectory is y = x tan θ − g x²/(2u² cos² θ). Comparing coefficients gives tan θ = 1 and g/(2u² cos² θ) = 0.05. The range, height and time then follow from the usual formulas, or directly from the equation (y = 0 again at x = 20 m).
steps: (c) y = 0 at x = 0 and x = 1/0.05 = 20 m → R = 20 m, true
(d) H = u² sin² θ/2g = 200 × ½/20 = 5 m (or y at x = 10 m = 10 − 5 = 5 m) → false
solution.shortcut: The maximum height occurs at half the range: y(10) = 10 − 0.05 × 100 = 5 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) doubles the true height; (e) forgets the factor sin 45° in the vertical component of velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion (equation of path)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a particle moving along a straight line with constant acceleration, its average velocity over a time interval equals its instantaneous velocity at the middle instant of that interval.
Reason (R): When the acceleration is constant, the velocity changes linearly with time, so the average of the velocities at the beginning and end of the interval is also the velocity at its mid-instant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Average velocity for uniformly accelerated motion
solution.explanation: With constant acceleration, v = u + at is linear in t. The displacement in time t is ut + ½at², so the average velocity is u + ½at, which is exactly the velocity at time t/2. The reason states the linearity that makes this true, so R correctly explains A.
steps: Velocity at t/2 = u + a(t/2) = u + ½at → equal
This depends on v being linear in t (constant a) → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not merely a related fact: if the acceleration were not constant, v(t) would not be linear and the average velocity would not in general equal the mid-instant velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A stone is dropped from rest into a well. The sound of the splash is heard 4.25 s after the stone is released. Taking g = 10 m/s², the speed of sound in air as 320 m/s and neglecting air resistance, the depth of the water surface below the point of release is:

solution.concept: Two successive motions: free fall, then sound returning at constant speed
solution.explanation: The total time is the time of fall, √(2h/g), plus the time the sound takes to come back up, h/v. The depth must satisfy both together; trying the value that makes the fall time a whole number of seconds shows h = 80 m works.
steps: Fall time t₁ = √(2h/10), sound time t₂ = h/320, t₁ + t₂ = 4.25 s
(Only one positive depth satisfies the condition, since t₁ + t₂ increases steadily with h.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 90.3 m ignores the time taken by the sound (½ × 10 × 4.25²); 45 m and 68 m do not give a total time of 4.25 s (they give 3.14 s and about 3.90 s).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground. It is at the same height above the ground at t = 2 s (going up) and at t = 4 s (coming down). Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The ball was thrown up with a speed of 30 m/s.
(b) The common height at t = 2 s and t = 4 s is 30 m.
(c) The maximum height reached by the ball is 45 m.
(d) The speed of the ball at t = 2 s is 20 m/s.
(e) The ball returns to the ground at t = 6 s.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Symmetry of vertical motion under gravity
solution.explanation: The ball is at its highest point midway between two instants at which it is at the same height, i.e. at t = 3 s. So u = g × 3 = 30 m/s. The rest follows from the equations of motion.
steps: Highest point at t = (2 + 4)/2 = 3 s → u = 10 × 3 = 30 m/s → (a) true
Height at t = 2 s: 30 × 2 − 5 × 4 = 40 m → (b) false
Speed at t = 2 s: 30 − 20 = 10 m/s → (d) false
solution.shortcut: For heights reached at t₁ and t₂: u = g(t₁ + t₂)/2 and h = g t₁t₂/2 = 5 × 2 × 4 = 40 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) takes the height as u × 1 s; (d) uses the speed lost in 1 s instead of 2 s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car moving at 20 m/s along a straight road is 50 m behind a truck moving in the same direction at a constant 10 m/s. At this instant the driver of the car applies the brakes, giving the car a uniform retardation. The least retardation that will just prevent the car from hitting the truck is:

solution.concept: Relative motion in one dimension with constant relative acceleration
solution.explanation: Work in the frame of the truck, which moves with constant velocity. Relative to the truck, the car starts 50 m behind with a speed of 10 m/s and decelerates at a. A collision is just avoided if the relative speed becomes zero exactly as the gap closes.
steps: Initial relative speed = 20 − 10 = 10 m/s; relative retardation = a (the truck does not accelerate)
Relative distance covered before relative rest = 10²/(2a)
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 m/s² applies (20² − 10²)/(2 × 50) using ground distances while ignoring that the truck also moves; 4 m/s² stops the car completely within 50 m; 0.5 m/s² is too small (the gap closes before the speeds become equal).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body of mass 2 kg moves along the x-axis so that its position is x = 3t² − 2t, where x is in metres and t in seconds. The net force acting on it is:

solution.concept: Newton's second law with acceleration found by differentiation
solution.explanation: Differentiate the position twice to get the acceleration; it is constant here, so the net force is constant.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 N omits the factor 2 on differentiating 3t² (takes a = 3 m/s²); 8 N uses the velocity 6t − 2 at t = 1 s as an acceleration and multiplies by 2; 24 N doubles the correct value.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block is pulled along a rough horizontal floor with a constant velocity by a horizontal force of 12 N. The frictional force acting on the block is:

options.text: 12 N, directed opposite to the motion
zero, since the block is not accelerating
more than 12 N, directed opposite to the motion

solution.concept: Newton's first law: constant velocity means zero net force
solution.explanation: The block moves with constant velocity, so its acceleration is zero and the net horizontal force on it is zero. The only horizontal forces are the pull and kinetic friction, so friction must be 12 N and opposite to the pull, i.e. opposite to the motion.
steps: 12 N (pull) − f = 0 → f = 12 N, opposite to the motion
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero acceleration means zero net force, not zero friction; friction larger than 12 N would decelerate the block; kinetic friction opposes the relative sliding, so it cannot point along the motion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's first law and friction
solution.final_answer: Option A: 12 N, directed opposite to the motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a rough horizontal floor. The least horizontal force needed just to start it moving is 40 N. Taking g = 10 m/s², the coefficient of static friction between the block and the floor is:

solution.concept: Limiting static friction: f_s(max) = μₛN
solution.explanation: The force that just starts the motion equals the limiting value of static friction, μₛN, with N = mg on a horizontal floor.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 divides the force by the mass instead of by the weight; 2.5 inverts the ratio (N/F); 0.25 divides the mass by the force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction (limiting static friction)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: On a smooth horizontal floor, block A of mass 2 kg moves at 6 m/s directly away from block B of mass 1 kg, which is at rest. The blocks are connected by a light inextensible string that is initially slack. When the string becomes taut, the two blocks are jerked into moving together with a common velocity. The magnitude of the impulse of the tension on block B during the jerk is:

solution.concept: Impulsive tension: momentum of the system conserved, impulse = change in momentum
solution.explanation: During the very short jerk, the only horizontal forces are the equal and opposite tensions at the two ends of the string, which are internal to the system. The total momentum is conserved, which gives the common velocity. The impulse on B equals its change of momentum.
steps: Check: impulse on A = 2 × (4 − 6) = −4 N s (equal and opposite)
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 N s gives B the initial speed of A; 2 N s is the impulse that would bring B only to 2 m/s; 12 N s is the initial momentum of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 8 kg rests on a rough horizontal table. It is tied to a light string that passes over a smooth, light pulley at the edge of the table and carries a hanging mass of 2 kg. The system stays at rest. The least coefficient of static friction between the block and the table for which this is possible is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium with static friction
solution.explanation: For the hanging mass at rest, the tension equals its weight. For the block at rest, static friction must balance this tension, and static friction cannot exceed μₛN with N equal to the block's weight.
steps: Friction needed on the 8 kg block = 20 N
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.2 divides by the total weight of both masses (100 N); 4 inverts the ratio; 0.5 halves the normal force.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A block of mass 2 kg lies on a rough horizontal floor; the coefficients of static and kinetic friction are 0.5 and 0.4. Take g = 10 m/s². A horizontal force P is applied to it, starting from rest. Match List-I (situation) with List-II (magnitude of the friction force on the block, or on the block and load together).

List-I:
A. P = 4 N
B. P = 9 N
C. P = 15 N
D. P = 20 N, with a 1 kg load fixed on top of the block

List-II:
I. 12 N
II. 9 N
III. 4 N
IV. 8 N

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Static friction is self-adjusting; kinetic friction is μₖN
solution.explanation: Limiting friction = μₛN = 0.5 × 20 = 10 N. While P is below this, the block stays at rest and static friction equals P. Once P exceeds the limit, the block slides and friction is kinetic, μₖN, whatever P is.
steps: P = 4 N < 10 N → at rest, f = 4 N (III)
P = 9 N < 10 N → at rest, f = 9 N (II)
P = 15 N > 10 N → slides, f = 0.4 × 20 = 8 N (IV)
With the load N = 30 N, limit = 15 N < 20 N → slides, f = 0.4 × 30 = 12 N (I)
solution.why_others_wrong: Taking friction as μₛN = 10 N or μₖN = 8 N in every case, or keeping f = P after the block has started to slide, leads to the other codes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', static and kinetic friction
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Newton's second law, in the form F = ma, is consistent with Newton's first law.
Reason (R): If the net external force on a body is zero, F = ma gives a = 0, so the body stays at rest or keeps moving with uniform velocity.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Relation between the first and second laws
solution.explanation: NCERT points out that the second law is consistent with the first: setting F = 0 in F = ma gives a = 0, which is exactly the statement of the first law. R shows why A holds, so it is the correct explanation.
steps: This is the content of the first law → A true, R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's second law of motion
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If a particle is in equilibrium under the action of three concurrent forces, the three forces must lie in one plane.
Statement II: A particle can be in equilibrium under the action of just two forces of magnitudes 5 N and 3 N.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Conditions for equilibrium of a particle
solution.explanation: Equilibrium requires the vector sum of the forces to be zero. With three forces, F₃ = −(F₁ + F₂), and F₁ + F₂ lies in the plane of F₁ and F₂, so F₃ lies in that plane too: Statement I is true. With two forces, equilibrium requires F₁ = −F₂, i.e. equal magnitudes; 5 N and 3 N can never cancel, so Statement II is false.
steps: Three forces: F₃ = −(F₁ + F₂) lies in the plane of F₁ and F₂ → I true
Two forces: need |F₁| = |F₂| and opposite → 5 N and 3 N cannot balance → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', equilibrium of a particle
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A conveyor belt moves horizontally with a constant speed of 4 m/s. A block of mass 2 kg is placed gently (at rest) on it. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the belt is 0.2. Taking g = 10 m/s², which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The block's acceleration while it slips on the belt is 2 m/s².
(b) The block slips on the belt for 2 s.
(c) The distance the block slides relative to the belt is 4 m.
(d) The work done by friction on the block is +16 J.
(e) While it slips, the block moves 8 m relative to the ground.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Kinetic friction accelerating a body to the speed of a moving surface
solution.explanation: Friction μₖmg acts forward on the block until it reaches the belt's speed. The block covers less ground than the belt in this time; the difference is the slip. Friction does positive work on the block equal to its gain of kinetic energy, while the heat produced is friction × relative sliding distance.
steps: (c) block moves ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 m, belt moves 4 × 2 = 8 m → slip = 4 m, true
(e) the block moves 4 m over the ground; 8 m is the distance moved by the belt → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) gives the belt's displacement (4 m/s × 2 s), not the block's; the block starts from rest and averages only 2 m/s while slipping. Every wrong option contains (e).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform chain lies straight on a rough horizontal table, perpendicular to the edge, with part of it hanging vertically over the edge. The coefficient of static friction between the chain and the table is 0.25. The largest fraction of the length of the chain that can hang over the edge without the chain beginning to slide is:

solution.concept: Limiting friction balancing the weight of the hanging part
solution.explanation: If a fraction f of the chain hangs, the weight of the hanging part, f Mg, pulls the chain. The part on the table, of weight (1 − f)Mg, can provide at most μₛ(1 − f)Mg of static friction. At the limit these are equal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 sets f = μₛ, forgetting that only the part on the table presses on it; 1/3 uses μₛ/(1 − μₛ); 4/5 is the fraction that stays on the table.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A block of mass m rests on the smooth inclined face of a wedge; the face makes 37° with the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). The wedge is pushed along a horizontal floor with a constant acceleration a, directed horizontally towards the side that the inclined face looks towards, so that the block stays at rest relative to the wedge. Take g = 10 m/s². Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The normal force exerted by the wedge on the block is 1.25 mg.
(b) The net force on the block is zero.
(c) The required acceleration a (7.5 m/s²) does not depend on the mass of the block.
(d) If the wedge were instead moved with constant velocity, the block would slide down the face with an acceleration of 6 m/s² relative to the wedge.
(e) The normal force exerted by the wedge on the block is 0.8 mg.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Newton's second law in the ground frame for a body accelerating with a wedge
solution.explanation: In the ground frame the block accelerates horizontally with a, so the net force on it is ma, horizontal. Only gravity and the normal force act (the face is smooth). The vertical component of N balances mg and the horizontal component supplies ma.
steps: Vertical: N cos 37° = mg → N = mg/0.8 = 1.25 mg → (a) true, (e) false
Horizontal: N sin 37° = ma → a = g tan 37° = 7.5 m/s², independent of m → (c) true
The block accelerates, so the net force is ma ≠ 0 → (b) false
Wedge moving uniformly (an inertial frame): block slides with g sin 37° = 6 m/s² → (d) true
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) confuses rest relative to the wedge with equilibrium; (e) is the normal force on a block resting on a fixed incline, where there is no horizontal acceleration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text: A ball of mass 2 kg is thrown vertically upward and rises through 5 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done on the ball by the force of gravity during this rise is:

solution.concept: Work done by a constant force: W = F d cos θ
solution.explanation: Gravity (mg, downward) and the displacement (5 m, upward) are opposite, so θ = 180° and the work done by gravity is negative.
steps: F = mg = 20 N downward, d = 5 m upward, θ = 180°
solution.why_others_wrong: +100 J ignores the angle between force and displacement; −10 J leaves out g (uses m × h); zero would need the force to be perpendicular to the displacement.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For a machine whose power output P varies with time t, the area under its power–time (P–t) graph between two instants gives:

options.text: the force exerted by the machine
the average power of the machine
the rate of doing work at the later instant
the work done by the machine in that interval

solution.concept: Power as the rate of doing work
solution.explanation: Instantaneous power is P = dW/dt, so the work done between t₁ and t₂ is W = ∫P dt, which is the area under the P–t graph between those instants.
steps: W = ∫ P dt = area under the P–t graph
solution.why_others_wrong: The average power is that area divided by the time interval, not the area itself; the rate of doing work at an instant is the ordinate P, not an area; force is not obtained from a P–t graph.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power
solution.final_answer: Option D: the work done by the machine in that interval

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
An ideal spring has spring constant 200 N/m. Match List-I with List-II (the energy or work).

List-I:
A. Potential energy stored when it is stretched 10 cm from its natural length
B. Work needed to increase its extension slowly from 10 cm to 20 cm
C. Potential energy stored when it is compressed 20 cm from its natural length
D. Potential energy stored when it is stretched 30 cm from its natural length

List-II:
I. 4 J
II. 9 J
III. 1 J
IV. 3 J

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Elastic potential energy of a spring: U = ½kx²
solution.explanation: The energy stored depends on the square of the extension or compression x, measured from the natural length, and not on whether the spring is stretched or compressed. The work needed to go from x₁ to x₂ is the difference ½k(x₂² − x₁²).
solution.why_others_wrong: Taking the extra 10 cm as starting from the natural length gives 1 J for B; treating energy as proportional to x (not x²) gives the other codes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body of mass 2 kg, initially at rest at the origin, moves along the x-axis so that its position is x = t³/3, where x is in metres and t in seconds. The work done by the net force on it during the first 2 s is:

solution.concept: Work–energy theorem: W_net = ΔK
solution.explanation: The net work equals the change in kinetic energy, so only the speeds at the two instants are needed.
steps: v = dx/dt = t² → v(0) = 0, v(2) = 4 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 J takes v = t (2 m/s at t = 2 s) instead of t²; 32 J forgets the ½ in the kinetic energy; 21.3 J multiplies the force at t = 2 s (m × 2t = 8 N) by the displacement 8/3 m, but the force is not constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A light vertical spring of spring constant 800 N/m is fixed to the floor and is held compressed by 5 cm from its natural length, with a ball of mass 0.1 kg resting on its top. The ball is released from rest and is thrown upward by the spring. Neglecting air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum height to which the ball rises above its point of release is:

solution.concept: Conservation of mechanical energy: elastic potential energy → gravitational potential energy
solution.explanation: The energy stored by the 5 cm compression is ½kx². The light spring keeps no kinetic energy, and at the highest point the ball is momentarily at rest, so all this energy has become gravitational potential energy mgh, measured from the point of release (this already includes the 5 cm rise while the spring extends).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 m forgets that the stored energy is already ½kx² and halves again; 2 m uses kx² without the ½; 0.95 m subtracts the 5 cm compression, but the height asked is measured from the release point itself.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car moving at a steady 20 m/s on a level road needs 10 kW of engine power to overcome air resistance, which is proportional to the square of its speed. Ignoring all other resistance, the power needed to keep it moving at a steady 40 m/s is:

solution.concept: Power at constant velocity: P = Fv
solution.explanation: At steady speed the driving force equals the resistive force, F = bv². The power is P = Fv = bv³, so it grows as the cube of the speed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 kW takes P ∝ v²; 20 kW takes P ∝ v; 160 kW takes P ∝ v⁴.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a block slides down a rough inclined plane, the decrease in its gravitational potential energy is greater than the increase in its kinetic energy.
Reason (R): The kinetic friction on the block does negative work, so part of the mechanical energy is converted into heat (internal energy) at the sliding surfaces.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Work–energy theorem with a non-conservative force
solution.explanation: By the work–energy theorem, ΔK = W_gravity + W_friction (the normal force does no work). W_gravity equals the loss of potential energy, and W_friction is negative, so ΔK is less than the loss of potential energy; the difference appears as heat. R gives exactly this cause.
steps: The negative work of friction is the cause → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the work–energy theorem and conservative forces
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small stone tied to a light inextensible string 1.0 m long hangs at rest. It is given a horizontal speed of √35 m/s at the lowest point so that it moves in a vertical circle. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the height above the lowest point at which the string becomes slack is:

solution.concept: Vertical circle: the string slackens where the tension becomes zero
solution.explanation: At an angle θ measured from the lowest position, energy conservation gives v² = u² − 2gL(1 − cos θ), and the radial equation gives T = mv²/L + mg cos θ. The string slackens where T = 0, which needs cos θ < 0 (above the horizontal through the centre).
steps: u² − 2gL + 2gL cos θ = −gL cos θ → cos θ = (2gL − u²)/(3gL)
Height above lowest point = L(1 − cos θ) = 1.5 m
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.75 m is u²/2g, the height at which the speed would become zero, but the string slackens earlier while the stone still moves; 2.0 m is the top of the circle, which needs u² ≥ 5gL = 50; 1.25 m does not make the tension zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body starts from rest on a smooth horizontal surface and is pushed by a machine that delivers a constant power to it. The ratio of the distance it covers in the first 1 s to the distance it covers in the first 4 s is:

solution.concept: Constant power: kinetic energy grows linearly with time
solution.explanation: With constant power P and no losses, ½mv² = Pt, so v = √(2Pt/m) ∝ t^(1/2). Integrating, the distance is x ∝ t^(3/2).
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 16 assumes uniform acceleration (x ∝ t²); 1 : 4 takes x ∝ t; 1 : 2 takes x ∝ √t, which is how the speed (not the distance) grows.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a very heavy body moving with speed u collides head-on and elastically with a very light body at rest, the light body moves off with a speed of nearly 2u.
Statement II: When a very light body moving with speed u collides head-on and elastically with a very heavy body at rest, the light body rebounds with a speed of nearly u and transfers nearly all of its kinetic energy to the heavy body.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: One-dimensional elastic collision with a target at rest: limiting cases
solution.explanation: For m₁ moving at u striking m₂ at rest: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂) and v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂). If m₁ ≫ m₂, v₂ ≈ 2u, so Statement I is true. If m₁ ≪ m₂, v₁ ≈ −u: the light body bounces back with almost its whole speed, so it keeps almost all its kinetic energy and the heavy body gains almost none. Statement II's second part is false.
steps: m₁ ≫ m₂: v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂) → 2u → I true
m₁ ≪ m₂: v₁ → −u, v₂ → 2m₁u/m₂ → 0 → kinetic energy transferred → 0 → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', collisions in one dimension
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A wheel starts from rest and rotates about a fixed axis with a uniform angular acceleration of 2 rad/s². Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (its value).

List-I:
A. Angular speed at t = 3 s
B. Angle turned through in the first 3 s
C. Angle turned through during the third second (from t = 2 s to t = 3 s)
D. Angular speed after it has turned through 16 rad

List-II:
I. 8 rad/s
II. 5 rad
III. 9 rad
IV. 6 rad/s

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Kinematic equations of rotational motion with constant angular acceleration
solution.explanation: With ω₀ = 0 and constant α: ω = αt, θ = ½αt² and ω² = 2αθ. These are the rotational analogues of the equations of uniformly accelerated linear motion.
solution.why_others_wrong: Confusing the angle in the first 3 s with the angle in the third second, or the angular speed at 3 s with that after 16 rad, gives the other codes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', kinematics of rotational motion about a fixed axis
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The centre of gravity of a body coincides with its centre of mass when:

options.text: the acceleration due to gravity has the same value at all points of the body
the body is a rigid body of any size
the body is symmetrical about a vertical axis

solution.concept: Centre of gravity and centre of mass
solution.explanation: The centre of gravity is the point about which the total gravitational torque on the body is zero. If g is the same at every point of the body, this condition becomes Σmᵢrᵢ = 0 about that point, which defines the centre of mass. For bodies small compared with the Earth this holds, so the two points coincide.
steps: Σ rᵢ × mᵢg = 0 about the centre of gravity
g uniform → (Σmᵢrᵢ) × g = 0 → Σmᵢrᵢ = 0 → centre of mass
solution.why_others_wrong: Rigidity, rest or symmetry about a vertical axis do not make the weights of all parts proportional to their masses; only a uniform g does.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', centre of gravity
solution.final_answer: Option A: the acceleration due to gravity has the same value at all points of the body

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A flywheel has a moment of inertia of 2 kg m² about its axle. The work needed to increase its angular speed from 10 rad/s to 20 rad/s is:

solution.concept: Work–energy theorem for rotation: W = ΔK = ½I(ω₂² − ω₁²)
solution.explanation: The work done by the torque equals the change in rotational kinetic energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 J uses ½I(ω₂ − ω₁)²; 400 J is the final kinetic energy alone; 600 J forgets the ½.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: Of all the axes parallel to a given direction, the moment of inertia of a rigid body is the least about the axis that:

options.text: is farthest from its centre of mass
passes through its centre of mass
touches the surface of the body
passes through its heaviest part, whatever the position of the centre of mass

solution.concept: Theorem of parallel axes
solution.explanation: By the theorem of parallel axes, I = I_cm + Md², where d is the distance of the axis from the parallel axis through the centre of mass. Since Md² ≥ 0, I is least when d = 0, i.e. for the axis through the centre of mass.
steps: Md² is smallest (zero) for d = 0 → axis through the centre of mass
solution.why_others_wrong: Moving the axis away from the centre of mass only adds Md²; a tangent is a particular parallel axis at d > 0, so it cannot give the minimum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', theorem of parallel axes
solution.final_answer: Option B: passes through its centre of mass

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: A thin uniform rod of mass 3 kg and length 2 m carries a small ball of mass 1 kg fixed at each end. The moment of inertia of this system about an axis perpendicular to the rod through its midpoint is:

solution.concept: Moment of inertia of a composite body: add the parts about the same axis
solution.explanation: The rod contributes ML²/12 about its perpendicular bisector; each ball, a point mass at distance L/2, contributes m(L/2)².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 kg m² is the rod alone; 2 kg m² is the balls alone; 5 kg m² uses ML²/3 for the rod (axis at an end).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A horizontal platform with moment of inertia 200 kg m² about its vertical axle is at rest and can turn freely. A child of mass 50 kg runs at 4 m/s along a tangent to the rim (radius 2 m) and jumps onto the rim. Treat the child as a particle. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The platform and child then rotate with an angular speed of 1 rad/s.
(b) The angular momentum of the child–platform system about the axle is conserved during the jump.
(c) The kinetic energy of the system is conserved during the jump.
(d) The linear momentum of the child–platform system is conserved during the jump.
(e) 200 J of kinetic energy is lost in the process.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum about a fixed axis
solution.explanation: The axle can exert forces but no torque about itself, so angular momentum about the axle is conserved. The child's angular momentum about the axle is mvR. The child 'sticks' to the platform, so kinetic energy is not conserved. Linear momentum is not conserved either, because the axle exerts an external horizontal force.
steps: I_total = 200 + 50 × 2² = 400 kg m² → ω = 1 rad/s → (a) true
No external torque about the axle → (b) true
K before = ½ × 50 × 16 = 400 J; K after = ½ × 400 × 1 = 200 J → (c) false, (e) true
Momentum before 200 kg m/s; after, only the child moves (at ωR = 2 m/s) → 100 kg m/s → (d) false
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) treats the jump as elastic; (d) ignores the force exerted by the fixed axle on the platform.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', conservation of angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a shell fired from a gun explodes in mid-air, the centre of mass of its fragments continues to move along the same parabolic path that the unexploded shell would have followed (until a fragment hits the ground).
Reason (R): The forces of the explosion are internal to the system of fragments, and the only external force, the total weight, is unchanged, so the acceleration of the centre of mass stays equal to g.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Motion of the centre of mass of a system: M a_cm = F_ext
solution.explanation: The centre of mass of a system moves as a particle of mass M acted on by the total external force. Internal forces, however large, cancel in pairs. Since the external force (gravity) is the same before and after the explosion, the centre of mass keeps the same acceleration and hence the same trajectory. R gives this cause, so it explains A.
steps: M a_cm = F_ext = Mg before and after the explosion
Internal forces cancel → path of CM unchanged
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', motion of centre of mass
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a uniform circular disc, the moment of inertia about a tangent lying in its plane is smaller than the moment of inertia about a tangent perpendicular to its plane.
Statement II: The radius of gyration of a thin uniform ring of radius R about any of its diameters is R/√2.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Theorems of parallel and perpendicular axes for a disc and a ring
solution.explanation: For a disc, I about a diameter is MR²/4 and about the central perpendicular axis MR²/2. Adding MR² by the parallel-axes theorem gives 5MR²/4 for a tangent in the plane and 3MR²/2 for a tangent perpendicular to the plane, so Statement I is true. For a ring, I about the central axis is MR², and by the perpendicular-axes theorem I about a diameter is MR²/2 = Mk², giving k = R/√2: Statement II is true.
steps: Disc: tangent in plane = MR²/4 + MR² = 1.25 MR²; tangent ⊥ plane = MR²/2 + MR² = 1.5 MR² → I true
Ring: I_diameter = MR²/2 → k = R/√2 → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', theorems of perpendicular and parallel axes
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wheel starts from rest and rotates about a fixed axle with a constant angular acceleration of 4 rad/s². At what time after the start does the total acceleration of a point on its rim make an angle of 45° with the radius through that point?

solution.concept: Tangential and centripetal components of acceleration in non-uniform rotation
solution.explanation: A point at distance r has a tangential acceleration αr (constant) and a centripetal acceleration ω²r directed along the radius. The total acceleration makes 45° with the radius when the two components are equal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.25 s takes t = 1/α; 1 s and 2 s give a centripetal component 4 and 16 times the tangential one.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform rod of weight 60√3 N has its lower end hinged smoothly to the floor. It is held at rest at 60° to the horizontal by a light horizontal string tied to its upper end and fixed to a vertical wall. The tension in the string is:

solution.concept: Rotational equilibrium: net torque about the hinge is zero
solution.explanation: Take torques about the hinge, so the unknown hinge force has no moment. The weight acts at the midpoint, at a horizontal distance (L/2) cos 60° from the hinge; the horizontal tension acts at the top, at a height L sin 60° above the hinge.
steps: Torque of tension = T L sin 60°
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 N interchanges sine and cosine (uses the rod's angle with the vertical); 60√3 N takes the tension equal to the weight; 30√3 N takes it as half the weight, ignoring the geometry.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The angular velocity of a wheel of moment of inertia 2 kg m² about its fixed axle varies with time as ω = 3t², where ω is in rad/s and t in seconds. The power delivered by the net torque on the wheel at t = 2 s is:

solution.concept: Rotational power: P = τω, with τ = I dω/dt
solution.explanation: The torque is found from the angular acceleration, and the instantaneous power is the product of torque and angular velocity. (Equivalently, P = dK/dt with K = ½Iω².)
steps: α = dω/dt = 6t → at t = 2 s, α = 12 rad/s²
solution.shortcut: K = ½ × 2 × 9t⁴ = 9t⁴ → P = dK/dt = 36t³ = 288 W at t = 2 s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 144 W is the kinetic energy at t = 2 s, not its rate of change; 24 W is the torque value; 576 W takes K = Iω² (forgetting the ½) before differentiating.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a planet that is a uniform sphere of density ρ and radius R, the acceleration due to gravity at its surface is proportional to the product ρR.
Statement II: A planet with twice the mean density of the Earth and half its radius has the same escape speed from its surface as the Earth.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: g and escape speed in terms of density and radius
solution.explanation: With M = (4/3)πR³ρ, g = GM/R² = (4/3)πGρR, so Statement I is true. For the planet, ρR is unchanged, so g is the same as on the Earth; but the escape speed is √(2gR), and R is halved, so the escape speed is 1/√2 times the Earth's. Statement II is false.
steps: vₑ = √(2gR) → R halved → vₑ becomes vₑ/√2 → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity of the Earth and escape speed
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body is taken to the centre of the Earth (treated as a uniform sphere). There, its mass and its weight are respectively:

solution.concept: Variation of g with depth
solution.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location. Inside a uniform Earth, g(d) = g(1 − d/R), which becomes zero at d = R (the centre). The weight mg is therefore zero there.
solution.why_others_wrong: Mass never becomes zero by moving a body; g does not become infinite at the centre (the 1/r² law holds only outside the Earth); the weight does change because g changes with depth.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity below the surface of the Earth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A satellite revolves round the Earth in a circular orbit at a height above the surface equal to the Earth's radius R. Take g as the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface and ignore the Earth's rotation. Match List-I (quantity for the satellite) with List-II (its value).

List-I:
A. Orbital speed
B. Acceleration of the satellite
C. Period of revolution
D. Speed needed at that height to escape from the Earth

List-II:
I. √(gR)
II. g/4
III. √(gR/2)
IV. 4π√(2R/g)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Satellite in a circular orbit of radius r = 2R, with GM = gR²
solution.explanation: The orbit radius is r = R + R = 2R. Use GM = gR². The orbital speed is √(GM/r), the acceleration is the local gravitational field GM/r², the period is 2πr/v, and the escape speed from distance r is √(2GM/r).
solution.shortcut: At the same distance, escape speed = √2 × orbital speed.
solution.why_others_wrong: Interchanging the orbital speed with the escape speed, or using g/2 (dividing by r instead of r²) for the acceleration, gives the other codes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', earth satellites and escape speed
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two point masses, each of mass m, are fixed at the points (−3 m, 0) and (3 m, 0). G is the universal gravitational constant. The magnitude of the gravitational field (intensity) due to them at the point (0, 4 m) is:

solution.concept: Superposition of gravitational fields (vector addition)
solution.explanation: Each mass is 5 m from the point, so each field has magnitude Gm/25 and points towards its mass. The x-components cancel by symmetry; the y-components (towards the line joining the masses) add.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6Gm/125 adds the x-components (cos factor 3/5) instead of the y-components; 2Gm/25 adds the magnitudes as if the fields were parallel; zero would hold only at the midpoint of the line joining the masses.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Taking the gravitational potential energy to be zero at infinity, the potential energy of a body of mass m at a height equal to the Earth's radius R above the surface is −mgR/2, where g is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface.
Reason (R): The acceleration due to gravity at a height R above the Earth's surface is g/2.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Gravitational potential energy at a distance r: U = −GMm/r
solution.explanation: At height R, r = 2R and U = −GMm/(2R) = −gR²m/(2R) = −mgR/2, so A is true. The acceleration due to gravity there is GM/(2R)² = g/4, not g/2, so R is false. (The potential falls off as 1/r, the field as 1/r².)
steps: U = −GMm/(2R), GM = gR² → U = −mgR/2 → A true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy and acceleration due to gravity above the surface
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: On the surface of a planet, the acceleration due to gravity is the same as on the Earth's surface, but the escape speed is twice that from the Earth. Treating both as uniform spheres and ignoring rotation, the mass of the planet is (Mₑ = mass of the Earth):

solution.concept: Escape speed vₑ = √(2gR) and surface gravity g = GM/R²
solution.explanation: Write the escape speed in terms of g and R. With g the same, a doubled escape speed needs a radius four times larger. Then M = gR²/G grows as R².
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 Mₑ takes M ∝ R (stops after finding the radius); 8 Mₑ assumes the radius is only doubled and the density unchanged (M ∝ R³); 2 Mₑ takes M proportional to the escape speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two particles of masses m and 4m are initially at rest very far apart in free space. They move towards each other only because of their mutual gravitational attraction. When the distance between them is r, the speed of the particle of mass m is (G is the universal gravitational constant):

solution.concept: Conservation of linear momentum and of energy for two gravitating particles
solution.explanation: No external force acts, so the total momentum stays zero: m v₁ = 4m v₂. The gain in total kinetic energy equals the loss of gravitational potential energy, G(m)(4m)/r.
solution.why_others_wrong: √(8Gm/r) gives all the energy to the lighter particle (ignores the heavy one's kinetic energy); √(10Gm/r) is their relative speed, (5/4)v₁; √(8Gm/5r) takes the potential energy as Gm²/r, forgetting the factor 4.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wire 4 m long with a cross-sectional area of 2 mm² is stretched by 1 mm when a force of 100 N is applied along its length. Young's modulus of the material of the wire is:

solution.concept: Young's modulus Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L)
solution.explanation: Young's modulus is the ratio of the tensile stress to the longitudinal strain, within the elastic limit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 × 10¹⁰ N/m² forgets to divide the extension by the length 4 m (uses strain 10⁻³); 2 × 10⁸ N/m² puts the extension in millimetres (1) instead of metres; 8 × 10¹¹ N/m² multiplies by the length twice.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A soap film is held in a rectangular wire frame of size 10 cm × 6 cm. One side of the frame is moved slowly so that the film becomes 10 cm × 8 cm, at constant temperature. The surface tension of the soap solution is 0.03 N/m. The work done in stretching the film is:

solution.concept: Surface energy: work = surface tension × increase in surface area
solution.explanation: Surface tension equals the surface energy per unit area. A soap film has two surfaces, front and back, so the total new surface area is twice the increase in the area of the frame.
steps: Increase in frame area = 10 cm × 2 cm = 20 cm² = 2 × 10⁻³ m²
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ J counts only one surface; 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ J counts four surfaces; 1.2 × 10⁻² J leaves the area in cm² while using S in N/m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', surface energy and surface tension

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For the steady, streamline flow of an ideal (incompressible, non-viscous) liquid through a horizontal pipe of varying cross-section, Bernoulli's equation takes the form:

options.text: P + ρgh = constant, whatever the speed
P − ½ρv² = constant along a streamline
P + ½ρv² = constant along a streamline

solution.concept: Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal streamline
solution.explanation: Bernoulli's principle states that P + ½ρv² + ρgh is the same at all points along a streamline in steady flow of an ideal fluid. In a horizontal pipe the height h is the same everywhere, so P + ½ρv² is constant: where the liquid moves faster, its pressure is lower.
steps: Horizontal pipe: ρgh same everywhere → P + ½ρv² = constant
solution.why_others_wrong: P + ρgh = constant is the law for a liquid at rest; Pv = constant has no basis (pressure and speed are not inversely proportional); P − ½ρv² would make the pressure rise where the liquid speeds up.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Bernoulli's principle
solution.final_answer: Option D: P + ½ρv² = constant along a streamline

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking the atmospheric pressure as 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, the density of water as 1000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s², the depth below the surface of a lake at which the absolute pressure is twice the atmospheric pressure is:

solution.concept: Pressure at a depth: P = P₀ + ρgh
solution.explanation: The absolute pressure at depth h is the atmospheric pressure plus the pressure of the water column above. It is 2P₀ when the water column alone supplies P₀.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 m makes the gauge pressure (ρgh) equal to 2P₀, forgetting the atmosphere's own contribution; 5 m halves it; 1 m drops a factor of 10.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', pressure (variation with depth)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A clean glass capillary tube of internal radius 0.5 mm is dipped vertically in water. The surface tension of water is 0.07 N/m and the angle of contact is zero. Taking g = 10 m/s² and π = 22/7, the mass of water raised in the tube above the outside water level (neglecting the small amount in the meniscus) is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium of the raised liquid column: upward surface-tension force = weight of column
solution.explanation: Around the circular line of contact of length 2πr, surface tension pulls the liquid up with a force 2πrS cos θ. In equilibrium this balances the weight mg of the raised column, so m = 2πrS cos θ/g, independent of the density and of the height.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 mg uses πrS (only half the contact line); 44 mg uses the diameter in 2πr; 2.2 mg slips a power of ten in converting kg to mg.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal block of mass 0.84 kg and specific heat capacity 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, at 100 °C, is placed in a cavity in a large block of ice at 0 °C, and the cavity is closed. The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg. Assuming no heat is lost, the mass of ice that melts is:

solution.concept: Calorimetry: heat lost by the hot body = heat used to melt ice
solution.explanation: The large block of ice stays at 0 °C, so the metal cools to 0 °C. All the heat it gives out melts ice at 0 °C, without changing its temperature.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 g and 1 kg slip a power of ten; 50 g takes the metal to cool only to 50 °C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A steel wire 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm² is stretched by 1 mm within its elastic limit. Young's modulus of steel is 2 × 10¹¹ N/m². The elastic potential energy stored in the wire is:

solution.concept: Elastic potential energy of a stretched wire: U = ½ × force × extension
solution.explanation: Within the elastic limit the wire behaves like a spring of force constant k = YA/L. The work done in stretching it, stored as elastic energy, is ½kx² (equivalently ½ × stress × strain × volume).
steps: Check: final force = kx = 100 N → U = ½ × 100 × 10⁻³ = 0.05 J
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 J forgets the ½ (uses force × extension); 0.025 J halves twice; 0.5 J slips a power of ten in the area.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', elastic potential energy in a stretched wire

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Within the elastic limit, doubling the load hung from a given wire doubles its extension.
Reason (R): Within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law); for a given wire the stress is proportional to the load and the strain to the extension.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Hooke's law applied to a stretched wire
solution.explanation: For a wire of cross-section A and length L, stress = F/A and strain = ΔL/L. Hooke's law (stress ∝ strain, i.e. F/A = Y ΔL/L) then gives ΔL = FL/(AY) ∝ F for the given wire. So doubling the load doubles the extension, and R is exactly the reason.
steps: A, L, Y fixed → ΔL ∝ F → doubling F doubles ΔL → A true, R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Hooke's law and Young's modulus
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The heat capacity of a body depends on its mass, whereas the specific heat capacity of its material does not.
Statement II: The coefficient of linear expansion of a material has the same numerical value whether it is expressed per °C or per K.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Heat capacity versus specific heat capacity; size of a temperature interval
solution.explanation: Heat capacity S = ΔQ/ΔT is the heat needed to raise the whole body by 1 K, so it is proportional to the mass; specific heat capacity s = S/m is a property of the substance. Statement I is true. A temperature change of 1 °C is the same as a change of 1 K, so α (fractional change in length per unit change of temperature) has the same value in either unit. Statement II is true.
steps: S = ms → depends on mass; s does not → I true
ΔT (°C) = ΔT (K) → α per °C = α per K → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', specific heat capacity and thermal expansion
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A load hung from a wire produces an extension e. The wire is replaced by another wire of the same material, with the changes listed in List-I (anything not mentioned is unchanged). Match List-I with List-II (the new extension, within the elastic limit).

List-I:
A. Length doubled
B. Diameter doubled
C. Length doubled and load halved
D. Length doubled and diameter halved

List-II:
I. e/4
II. e
III. 2e
IV. 8e

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Extension of a wire: e = FL/(AY) = 4FL/(πd²Y)
solution.explanation: For the same material, Y is fixed, so the extension is proportional to the load and the length and inversely proportional to the square of the diameter.
solution.why_others_wrong: Treating the extension as inversely proportional to the diameter (not its square) gives 2e for B and 4e for D, which leads to the wrong codes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Young's modulus
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A horizontal syringe filled with water has a piston of cross-sectional area 1 cm² and a very narrow nozzle open to the atmosphere. The piston is pushed steadily with a force of 3.2 N. Treating water (density 1000 kg/m³) as an ideal fluid in steady flow and neglecting the speed of the water inside the barrel, the speed with which water comes out of the nozzle is:

solution.concept: Bernoulli's equation between the barrel and the nozzle
solution.explanation: Inside the barrel the pressure exceeds atmospheric by F/A. At the nozzle the pressure is atmospheric. Both points are at the same height, and the speed in the wide barrel is negligible, so all the excess pressure becomes kinetic energy per unit volume at the nozzle.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.7 m/s uses v² = ΔP/ρ (drops the ½); 64 m/s is v², not v; 4 m/s halves the excess pressure.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Bernoulli's principle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal block of mass 0.25 kg at 140 °C is dropped into a calorimeter of heat capacity 80 J/K containing 0.1 kg of water at 20 °C. The final common temperature is 40 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and no heat is lost to the surroundings. The specific heat capacity of the metal is:

solution.concept: Principle of calorimetry including the calorimeter
solution.explanation: Heat lost by the metal equals heat gained by the water and the calorimeter together, both of which warm from 20 °C to 40 °C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 336 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ ignores the heat taken by the calorimeter; 200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ doubles the mass of the metal; 800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ halves it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: One end of a copper rod, 0.4 m long and of cross-sectional area 4 cm², is kept in steam at 100 °C and the other end in a large block of ice at 0 °C. The sides of the rod are insulated. The thermal conductivity of copper is 400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ and the latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg. In the steady state, the mass of ice melted in 7 minutes is:

solution.concept: Steady-state conduction H = KA(T₁ − T₂)/L, followed by latent heat
solution.explanation: In the steady state the rate of heat flow is the same at every section of the rod. All the heat arriving at the cold end melts ice at 0 °C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 g doubles the area or the time; 0.83 g uses 7 s instead of 7 minutes (time not converted to seconds); 5 g takes the area as 0.4 cm², slipping a power of ten.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A clean glass capillary tube of internal radius 0.05 mm is held vertically with its lower end in water. The surface tension of water is 0.07 N/m, its density 1000 kg/m³ and the angle of contact zero; take g = 10 m/s². The tube is long enough in every case. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Water rises 28 cm in the tube.
(b) In a tube of internal radius 0.2 mm of the same glass, water would rise 7 cm.
(c) The height of rise does not depend on the density of the liquid.
(d) If the same experiment were done on the Moon (g one-sixth of that on the Earth), water would rise 168 cm in the 0.05 mm tube.
(e) Adding a detergent to the water would make it rise higher in the tube.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Capillary rise: h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr)
solution.explanation: The height of rise is inversely proportional to the radius, the density and g, and proportional to the surface tension (for θ = 0).
steps: (b) radius 4 times larger → h = 28/4 = 7 cm, true
(e) detergent lowers the surface tension → the rise decreases → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) forgets that the weight of the raised column, which balances surface tension, depends on ρ; (e) has the effect of detergents the wrong way round.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', capillary rise

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A gas expands adiabatically and does 300 J of work on its surroundings. The change in its internal energy is:

solution.concept: First law of thermodynamics for an adiabatic process (ΔQ = 0)
solution.explanation: In the form ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW (ΔW = work done by the system), an adiabatic process has ΔQ = 0, so ΔU = −ΔW. The work done by the gas comes entirely from its internal energy.
steps: ΔU = ΔQ − ΔW = −300 J (the gas cools)
solution.why_others_wrong: +300 J reverses the sign convention; zero would be the isothermal case for an ideal gas; −150 J halves the work for no reason.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics and adiabatic process

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about heat is correct, in the sense used in thermodynamics?

options.text: A hot body contains a large amount of heat
Heat is energy that flows between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference
Heat, like internal energy, is a state variable
Heat can flow only by doing mechanical work

solution.concept: Heat, work and internal energy
solution.explanation: Internal energy is a property of the state of a system. Heat and work are not; they are two modes of transferring energy. Heat is the energy transferred because of a temperature difference. A body contains internal energy, not 'heat'.
steps: Heat ΔQ and work ΔW: energy in transit, depend on the path
solution.why_others_wrong: A body has internal energy, not a store of heat; heat depends on the path and so is not a state variable; heat transfer due to a temperature difference does not need mechanical work.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', heat, internal energy and work
solution.final_answer: Option B: Heat is energy that flows between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A gas is taken once, clockwise, round a closed cycle that appears on a P–V diagram as an ellipse. The pressure in the cycle varies between 1 × 10⁵ Pa and 3 × 10⁵ Pa and the volume between 1 L and 3 L, the ellipse having its axes parallel to the P and V axes. The net work done by the gas in one cycle is:

solution.concept: Work in a cyclic process = area enclosed on the P–V diagram
solution.explanation: For a cycle traversed clockwise on a P–V diagram (V horizontal), the net work done by the gas is positive and equal to the enclosed area. An ellipse with semi-axes a and b has area πab.
solution.why_others_wrong: 400 J is the area of the bounding rectangle; 400π J uses the full axes (2 × 10⁵ Pa and 2 L) instead of the semi-axes; 50π J halves the area.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', work done in a cyclic process (area on the P–V diagram)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
An ideal gas is enclosed in a rigid, thermally insulated container. A paddle wheel inside, driven from outside, stirs the gas, and in this way 500 J of work is done on the gas. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) No heat is exchanged between the gas and its surroundings.
(b) The internal energy of the gas increases by 500 J.
(c) The temperature of the gas rises.
(d) The process is reversible: turning the paddle backwards would cool the gas back to its initial state.
(e) The gas does 500 J of work on the paddle.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: First law with work done on a system; dissipative processes are irreversible
solution.explanation: The walls are insulating, so ΔQ = 0. Work is done on the gas, so in ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW we have ΔW = −500 J and ΔU = +500 J. For an ideal gas U depends only on T, so T rises. Stirring is a dissipative process: turning the paddle the other way also heats the gas, so the process cannot be reversed.
steps: (c) U rises → T rises (ideal gas), true
(e) work is done ON the gas (ΔW = −500 J), not by it, false
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) ignores that dissipative effects such as viscous stirring make a process irreversible; (e) reverses the direction of the energy transfer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law and reversible and irreversible processes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Second law, reversible and irreversible processes
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, all the heat absorbed by the gas is converted into work.
Statement II: This does not contradict the Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law, because the conversion of heat into work is not the sole result of the process: the gas ends up in a different state, with a larger volume.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: First law for an isothermal process and the wording of the Kelvin–Planck statement
solution.explanation: For an ideal gas U depends only on T, so in an isothermal process ΔU = 0 and ΔQ = ΔW: all the heat absorbed becomes work. Statement I is true. The Kelvin–Planck statement forbids a process whose SOLE result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and its complete conversion into work. Here the gas is left expanded, so the conversion is not the sole result; Statement II is true.
steps: Isothermal, ideal gas: ΔU = 0 → ΔQ = ΔW → I true
Kelvin–Planck forbids complete conversion as the sole result; here the state of the gas changes → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', second law of thermodynamics
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated so that throughout the process its volume is proportional to the square of its absolute temperature (V ∝ T²). Its temperature rises by 100 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and Cᵥ = 3R/2, the heat absorbed by the gas is:

solution.concept: First law with work computed for a given process
solution.explanation: Write V = kT². With PV = nRT, P = nRT/V, so the work in a small step is P dV = (nRT/kT²)(2kT dT) = 2nR dT. The total work is 2nRΔT; the change in internal energy is nCᵥΔT whatever the process.
solution.shortcut: The molar heat capacity of this process is Cᵥ + 2R = 3.5R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2490 J is ΔU alone; 4150 J is the heat at constant pressure (2.5R per mole), for which W would be nRΔT; 3320 J is the work alone.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A gas is enclosed in a horizontal cylinder by a light, frictionless piston of area 0.01 m². The outside of the piston is attached to a spring of spring constant 2000 N/m and is open to the atmosphere (pressure 1 × 10⁵ Pa). Initially the spring is at its natural length and the gas is at atmospheric pressure. The gas is heated slowly until the piston has moved out by 0.1 m. The work done by the gas is:

solution.concept: Work done by a gas against the atmosphere and a spring in a quasi-static process
solution.explanation: For a light piston moving slowly, the gas pressure always balances the atmospheric pressure plus the spring force per unit area. The work done by the gas is therefore the work done against the atmosphere plus the elastic energy stored in the spring.
steps: Stored in spring: ½kx² = ½ × 2000 × 0.01 = 10 J
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 J ignores the spring; 10 J ignores the atmosphere; 120 J uses kx² for the spring energy (forgets the ½).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A rigid, thermally insulated container is divided by a partition. One part holds 1 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at 400 K and the other 1 mol of a diatomic ideal gas (rigid molecules) at 240 K. The partition is removed and the gases mix without reacting. Using Cᵥ = 3R/2 and 5R/2 respectively, the final temperature is:

solution.concept: First law for an isolated system: total internal energy is conserved
solution.explanation: The container is rigid (no work) and insulated (no heat), so the total internal energy does not change. For an ideal gas U = nCᵥT, so the final temperature is the Cᵥ-weighted mean, not the simple mean.
solution.why_others_wrong: 320 K is the simple average of 400 K and 240 K; 340 K swaps the weights (2.5R with 400 K and 1.5R with 240 K); 306.7 K weights by Cₚ (2.5R and 3.5R), but no work is done in a rigid container, so Cᵥ applies.

questions.subject: Physics
